header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, .claude/settings.local.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: ShareOnboardingGuide

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. The cache is positional: agent() calls replay from cache up to the first call that failed, no longer matches the earlier run (edited, added, removed or reordered) or never started in it; that call and every call after it run again, even when their own (prompt, opts) are unchanged. ![Site frequency spectrum at several times after a crash and after growth](figures/sfs.png)

- Before either event, the spectrum lies along 1, as theory predicts.
- **At the end of a crash** (generation 20), singletons are at about 0.35 × their steady
  share and common variants at about 2 ×: the crash lost the rare variants first. Too few
  rare variants makes D positive.
- **After the crash** (generation 100), the tilt reverses: singletons are *above* their
  steady share (1.34 ×) and middle frequencies below it. The crash removed most of the old
  variation, and every new mutation starts as a singleton, so new rare variants make up
  more of what is left. This is why D dips below zero while the population recovers.
- **After growth**, singletons climb to 1.8 × their steady share by generation 100 and 2 ×
  by generation 500, while every other class falls below 1. A large population gains many
  new mutations each generation, and they have not had time to drift to higher
  frequencies. This is the negative D.

Recovery times vary by up to about a hundred generations from one random seed to the next
after crashes (more after growth, up to several hundred),
and depend on the number of simulated populations (more populations can detect smaller
leftover differences), so they should be compared at the same settings.

### Working backwards: what happened to this population?

The results above run forwards: given a history, what does variation look like? A real
study works backwards: it has **one sample** of sequences and asks what happened.
`inference.py` answers this with Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC):

1. **Reference table.** Simulate 200 populations for each of 21 histories (steady; crashes
   to N = 10, 20, 40 or 100 lasting 5, 10, 20 or 40 generations; growth to N = 400, 1000,
   2000 or 4000 over 20 generations), and sample each one every 10 generations for 1000
   generations. This gives 424,200 samples whose history is known. The time since the
   event costs nothing extra: one simulation, sampled at many times, covers them all.
2. **Compare.** Each sample is summarized by π, S and the number of singletons, which
   together capture the shape of the site frequency spectrum. Each is divided by its spread
   among steady samples, so the three are on a common scale.
3. **Keep the closest.** The 500 reference samples nearest the observed one show which
   histories could have produced it. Steady, crash and growth start with equal odds.

To test it, 9,000 reference samples (3,000 each of steady, crash and growth) were each
treated as an observation, and their history was inferred from the rest of the table, after
removing every sample from the same simulated population so no near-copy was left to find:

![How often one sample reveals the right history, and one worked example](figures/inference.png)

- **Severe crashes are clear; mild ones are invisible.** Crashes of strength above 1 are
  recognized 98% of the time in the first 300 generations, strong ones (0.4–1) 84%, but
  moderate (0.1–0.4) and weak (below 0.1) ones only 48% and 34%. A mild crash leaves a sample
  that looks steady, so a third of truly steady samples are also blamed on mild crashes
  (66% are called steady).
- **The crash signal fades** as the population recovers, in line with the recovery times
  above. **Growth gets easier to see with time** (75% in the first 300 generations, 98%
  after 600), because the excess of rare variants keeps building.
- **Strength, not depth or length.** In the worked example (right), the most likely cells
  are at the true strength, 0.5. The method can estimate the strength
  length / (2 × crash size), but not the depth and length separately, as the crash
  strength results above predict.
- **The uncertainty is honest.** The 90% ranges contain the true crash strength 97% of the
  time and the true time since the event 92% of the time. Single samples are noisy, though:
  the typical error in time since a crash is about 220 generations (80 after growth).

Two limits: the reference table assumes the sample was taken with the same N, μ and n,
and, like the rest of this project, that sites drift independently (see the app section).

## Setup

Requires Python 3.10 or newer.

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv          # on Debian/Ubuntu, first: sudo apt install python3-venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
```

## Interactive app

The app is online at https://dqy5p6gtahng9wvgfeyyst.streamlit.app/, hosted free on Streamlit
Community Cloud, which rebuilds it from this repository's `main` branch after every push. It
runs slower there than on a fast computer. To run it yourself:

```bash
.venv/bin/streamlit run app.py
```

This opens the app in your browser. It has two modes, chosen at the top of the sidebar.

**Explore an event.** Pick a steady, crash or growth history in the sidebar
(normal and event population size, event length, mutation rate, sample size, number of
populations), then press **Run simulation** (about 5–30 seconds; a progress bar shows how far
it has got, and settings that were already simulated come back at once). The app simulates the
event alongside a steady control and shows:

- **Averages over time:** Tajima's D, π, θ_W and S averaged over the populations, with the
  generation at which the event can no longer be told apart from the control. For π, dotted
  lines show the theory's prediction.
- **Site frequency spectrum:** an animation of the spectrum of the event and the control,
  relative to a steady population's (as in the figure above). Press **▶ Play** to watch
  rare variants vanish during a crash and return as the population recovers, or drag the
  slider. A small chart of population size above it marks the generation shown.
- **Single samples:** how often one sample from one population has a D outside the middle
  95% of D values in the steady control, and an animated histogram of D across populations
  over time.
- **Data:** the numbers behind the charts, including the theory's π.

**Work backwards.** Infers the history from one sample (see above). Either let the app
simulate a **mystery population** (it picks a random history and shows one sample's π, S
and singletons; press **Reveal the truth** afterwards), or **enter your own numbers**. The
app shows the chance of steady, crash and growth, the likely strength (or size after
growth) and time since the event, and a heat map of the possibilities. The reference table
for these settings is included in `inference_cache/`, so this mode starts at once; tables for
other settings take about a minute to build and are then saved there too.

The simulation lets every site drift independently, as if sites were unlinked. This gives
the right averages, but D varies less from population to population than Tajima's test
assumes (it assumes linked sites with no recombination). Tajima's standard limits would
therefore almost never flag a sample, so the app takes its limits from the simulated
steady control instead. The app shows Tajima's limits alongside for comparison.

## Running

| Command | What it does | Time |
|---|---|---|
| `.venv/bin/python plots.py` | Makes all seven figures in `figures/` | ~16 min |
| `.venv/bin/python plots.py crash` | Only the crash figure | ~15 s |
| `.venv/bin/python plots.py growth` | Only the growth figure | ~50 s |
| `.venv/bin/python plots.py severity` | Only the recovery time vs. crash size figure, plus its CSV | ~1 min |
| `.venv/bin/python plots.py length` | Only the crash length vs. depth figure, plus its CSV | ~2 min |
| `.venv/bin/python plots.py growthsize` | Only the recovery time vs. growth size figure, plus its CSV | ~10 min |
| `.venv/bin/python plots.py sfs` | Only the site frequency spectrum figure | ~25 s |
| `.venv/bin/python plots.py inference` | Only the working-backwards figure | ~1.5 min (+45 s the first time) |
| `.venv/bin/python inference.py` | Builds the reference table, infers four mystery populations and prints the validation | ~1 min (+45 s the first time) |
| `.venv/bin/python recovery.py` | Prints recovery times for crashes of several sizes | ~20 s |
| `.venv/bin/python diversity.py` | Prints average Tajima's D over time for steady, crash and growth | ~5 s |
| `.venv/bin/python infinite_sites.py` | Runs one population to equilibrium and prints its variation | <1 s |
| `.venv/bin/python wright_fisher.py` | Single-locus drift demos | <1 s |

Times are for an 8-core computer. The severity, length and growthsize figures repeat their
experiment with 5 random seeds, which run at the same time on different CPU cores; with
fewer cores they take longer, but give exactly the same results.

## Tests

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m unittest -v test_wright_fisher test_infinite_sites test_diversity test_recovery test_inference test_app test_animation
```

The 86 tests take about 30 seconds. Besides unit tests with hand-worked answers, they check
the simulation against population-genetics theory:

- A neutral allele fixes with probability equal to its starting frequency.
- Heterozygosity shrinks by a factor of (1 − 1/2N) each generation, through a crash.
- With mutation, total heterozygosity follows H′ = (1 − 1/2N)(H + 2μ) and levels off at 4Nμ − 2μ.
- In a steady population, E[π] = E[θ_W] = 4Nμ and Tajima's D averages about 0.
- Tajima's D is positive just after a crash and negative after rapid growth.
- The 5% limits of Tajima's test are near ±1.96 for large samples and widen at stricter levels.
- Limits taken from one set of steady populations flag about 5% of a new set.
- After growth, π recovers against a control at the new size but never against one at the old size.
- The theory for π (`expected_sample_pi`) equals 4Nμ at equilibrium and matches simulated
  samples through a crash.
- In a steady population the site frequency spectrum matches θ/i in every class; just
  after a crash singletons are too few, and during growth too many.
- Running seeds in parallel gives exactly the same recovery times as running them one
  after another.
- The app runs even when a crash leaves fewer gene copies than the usual sample size:
  the sample size is limited to 2N during a crash (`test_app.py` drives the real app), and
  shows both animations, also when the same settings are run again.
- Each animation has one frame per recorded generation, fixed axes, and frames that
  match the simulated numbers.
- Working backwards finds a recent severe crash and large growth from single samples, and
  gives each kind 1/3 prior odds even though the grid has more crash histories.

## How it works

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `wright_fisher.py` | One locus, two alleles: one generation of drift, population size histories (`make_crash_history`, `make_growth_history`), fixation probability. Also holds the shared random number generator (`set_seed`). |
| `infinite_sites.py` | Many sites under the infinite-sites model: every mutation hits a new site. `sites_generation_many` advances many independent populations in one NumPy call. `expected_sample_pi` predicts the average π for any population size history from theory alone. |
| `diversity.py` | Samples n sequences without replacement and computes S, π, θ_W and Tajima's D. `average_sample_stats` averages them over many populations at chosen generations; `sample_stats_per_trial` keeps each population's values. `tajima_critical_values` gives the limits of Tajima's test, and `control_limits` the limits from simulated steady populations. `sample_stats_and_sfs` also averages the site frequency spectrum, and `sfs_ratio` compares its shape with a steady population's. |
| `recovery.py` | Compares event populations with one steady control and finds the recovery time: the first generation after which they stay within 4 standard errors of each other. The control can be a different size from the starting population (`control_size`), which `growth_recovery_times` uses to compare grown populations with a control at the new size. `run_in_parallel` runs independent seeds on separate CPU cores; each seed sets its own random numbers, so the results are the same as running them one after another. |
| `inference.py` | Works backwards from one sample: builds the reference table (`build_reference_table`, saved in `inference_cache/`), keeps the closest simulated samples (`infer`), summarizes them (`summarize`) and tests the method on samples with known histories (`validate`). |
| `plots.py` | Draws the figures above. |
| `app.py` | The interactive Streamlit app. |
| `animation.py` | Builds the app's animated Plotly charts (the site frequency spectrum and the spread of D over time), with play and pause buttons, a slider and a time marker. |

![Site frequency spectrum at several times after a crash and after growth](figures/sfs.png)

- Before either event, the spectrum lies along 1, as theory predicts.
- **At the end of a crash** (generation 20), singletons are at about 0.35 × their steady
  share and common variants at about 2 ×: the crash lost the rare variants first. Too few
  rare variants makes D positive.
- **After the crash** (generation 100), the tilt reverses: singletons are *above* their
  steady share (1.34 ×) and middle frequencies below it. The crash removed most of the old
  variation, and every new mutation starts as a singleton, so new rare variants make up
  more of what is left. This is why D dips below zero while the population recovers.
- **After growth**, singletons climb to 1.8 × their steady share by generation 100 and 2 ×
  by generation 500, while every other class falls below 1. A large population gains many
  new mutations each generation, and they have not had time to drift to higher
  frequencies. This is the negative D.

Recovery times vary by up to about a hundred generations from one random seed to the next
after crashes (more after growth, up to several hundred),
and depend on the number of simulated populations (more populations can detect smaller
leftover differences), so they should be compared at the same settings.

### Working backwards: what happened to this population?

The results above run forwards: given a history, what does variation look like? A real
study works backwards: it has **one sample** of sequences and asks what happened.
`inference.py` answers this with Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC):

1. **Reference table.** Simulate 200 populations for each of 21 histories (steady; crashes
   to N = 10, 20, 40 or 100 lasting 5, 10, 20 or 40 generations; growth to N = 400, 1000,
   2000 or 4000 over 20 generations), and sample each one every 10 generations for 1000
   generations. This gives 424,200 samples whose history is known. The time since the
   event costs nothing extra: one simulation, sampled at many times, covers them all.
2. **Compare.** Each sample is summarized by π, S and the number of singletons, which
   together capture the shape of the site frequency spectrum. Each is divided by its spread
   among steady samples, so the three are on a common scale.
3. **Keep the closest.** The 500 reference samples nearest the observed one show which
   histories could have produced it. Steady, crash and growth start with equal odds.

To test it, 9,000 reference samples (3,000 each of steady, crash and growth) were each
treated as an observation, and their history was inferred from the rest of the table, after
removing every sample from the same simulated population so no near-copy was left to find:

![How often one sample reveals the right history, and one worked example](figures/inference.png)

- **Severe crashes are clear; mild ones are invisible.** Crashes of strength above 1 are
  recognized 98% of the time in the first 300 generations, strong ones (0.4–1) 84%, but
  moderate (0.1–0.4) and weak (below 0.1) ones only 48% and 34%. A mild crash leaves a sample
  that looks steady, so a third of truly steady samples are also blamed on mild crashes
  (66% are called steady).
- **The crash signal fades** as the population recovers, in line with the recovery times
  above. **Growth gets easier to see with time** (75% in the first 300 generations, 98%
  after 600), because the excess of rare variants keeps building.
- **Strength, not depth or length.** In the worked example (right), the most likely cells
  are at the true strength, 0.5. The method can estimate the strength
  length / (2 × crash size), but not the depth and length separately, as the crash
  strength results above predict.
- **The uncertainty is honest.** The 90% ranges contain the true crash strength 97% of the
  time and the true time since the event 92% of the time. Single samples are noisy, though:
  the typical error in time since a crash is about 220 generations (80 after growth).

Two limits: the reference table assumes the sample was taken with the same N, μ and n,
and, like the rest of this project, that sites drift independently (see the app section).

## Setup

Requires Python 3.10 or newer.

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv          # on Debian/Ubuntu, first: sudo apt install python3-venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
```

## Interactive app

The app is online at https://dqy5p6gtahng9wvgfeyyst.streamlit.app/, hosted free on Streamlit
Community Cloud, which rebuilds it from this repository's `main` branch after every push. It
runs slower there than on a fast computer. To run it yourself:

```bash
.venv/bin/streamlit run app.py
```

This opens the app in your browser. It has two modes, chosen at the top of the sidebar.

**Explore an event.** Pick a steady, crash or growth history in the sidebar
(normal and event population size, event length, mutation rate, sample size, number of
populations), then press **Run simulation** (about 5–30 seconds; a progress bar shows how far
it has got, and settings that were already simulated come back at once). The app simulates the
event alongside a steady control and shows:

- **Averages over time:** Tajima's D, π, θ_W and S averaged over the populations, with the
  generation at which the event can no longer be told apart from the control. For π, dotted
  lines show the theory's prediction.
- **Site frequency spectrum:** an animation of the spectrum of the event and the control,
  relative to a steady population's (as in the figure above). Press **▶ Play** to watch
  rare variants vanish during a crash and return as the population recovers, or drag the
  slider. A small chart of population size above it marks the generation shown.
- **Single samples:** how often one sample from one population has a D outside the middle
  95% of D values in the steady control, and an animated histogram of D across populations
  over time.
- **Data:** the numbers behind the charts, including the theory's π.

**Work backwards.** Infers the history from one sample (see above). Either let the app
simulate a **mystery population** (it picks a random history and shows one sample's π, S
and singletons; press **Reveal the truth** afterwards), or **enter your own numbers**. The
app shows the chance of steady, crash and growth, the likely strength (or size after
growth) and time since the event, and a heat map of the possibilities. The reference table
for these settings is included in `inference_cache/`, so this mode starts at once; tables for
other settings take about a minute to build and are then saved there too.

The simulation lets every site drift independently, as if sites were unlinked. This gives
the right averages, but D varies less from population to population than Tajima's test
assumes (it assumes linked sites with no recombination). Tajima's standard limits would
therefore almost never flag a sample, so the app takes its limits from the simulated
steady control instead. The app shows Tajima's limits alongside for comparison.

## Running

| Command | What it does | Time |
|---|---|---|
| `.venv/bin/python plots.py` | Makes all seven figures in `figures/` | ~16 min |
| `.venv/bin/python plots.py crash` | Only the crash figure | ~15 s |
| `.venv/bin/python plots.py growth` | Only the growth figure | ~50 s |
| `.venv/bin/python plots.py severity` | Only the recovery time vs. crash size figure, plus its CSV | ~1 min |
| `.venv/bin/python plots.py length` | Only the crash length vs. depth figure, plus its CSV | ~2 min |
| `.venv/bin/python plots.py growthsize` | Only the recovery time vs. growth size figure, plus its CSV | ~10 min |
| `.venv/bin/python plots.py sfs` | Only the site frequency spectrum figure | ~25 s |
| `.venv/bin/python plots.py inference` | Only the working-backwards figure | ~1.5 min (+45 s the first time) |
| `.venv/bin/python inference.py` | Builds the reference table, infers four mystery populations and prints the validation | ~1 min (+45 s the first time) |
| `.venv/bin/python recovery.py` | Prints recovery times for crashes of several sizes | ~20 s |
| `.venv/bin/python diversity.py` | Prints average Tajima's D over time for steady, crash and growth | ~5 s |
| `.venv/bin/python infinite_sites.py` | Runs one population to equilibrium and prints its variation | <1 s |
| `.venv/bin/python wright_fisher.py` | Single-locus drift demos | <1 s |

Times are for an 8-core computer. The severity, length and growthsize figures repeat their
experiment with 5 random seeds, which run at the same time on different CPU cores; with
fewer cores they take longer, but give exactly the same results.

## Tests

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m unittest -v test_wright_fisher test_infinite_sites test_diversity test_recovery test_inference test_app test_animation
```

The 86 tests take about 30 seconds. Besides unit tests with hand-worked answers, they check
the simulation against population-genetics theory:

- A neutral allele fixes with probability equal to its starting frequency.
- Heterozygosity shrinks by a factor of (1 − 1/2N) each generation, through a crash.
- With mutation, total heterozygosity follows H′ = (1 − 1/2N)(H + 2μ) and levels off at 4Nμ − 2μ.
- In a steady population, E[π] = E[θ_W] = 4Nμ and Tajima's D averages about 0.
- Tajima's D is positive just after a crash and negative after rapid growth.
- The 5% limits of Tajima's test are near ±1.96 for large samples and widen at stricter levels.
- Limits taken from one set of steady populations flag about 5% of a new set.
- After growth, π recovers against a control at the new size but never against one at the old size.
- The theory for π (`expected_sample_pi`) equals 4Nμ at equilibrium and matches simulated
  samples through a crash.
- In a steady population the site frequency spectrum matches θ/i in every class; just
  after a crash singletons are too few, and during growth too many.
- Running seeds in parallel gives exactly the same recovery times as running them one
  after another.
- The app runs even when a crash leaves fewer gene copies than the usual sample size:
  the sample size is limited to 2N during a crash (`test_app.py` drives the real app), and
  shows both animations, also when the same settings are run again.
- Each animation has one frame per recorded generation, fixed axes, and frames that
  match the simulated numbers.
- Working backwards finds a recent severe crash and large growth from single samples, and
  gives each kind 1/3 prior odds even though the grid has more crash histories.

## How it works

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `wright_fisher.py` | One locus, two alleles: one generation of drift, population size histories (`make_crash_history`, `make_growth_history`), fixation probability. Also holds the shared random number generator (`set_seed`). |
| `infinite_sites.py` | Many sites under the infinite-sites model: every mutation hits a new site. `sites_generation_many` advances many independent populations in one NumPy call. `expected_sample_pi` predicts the average π for any population size history from theory alone. |
| `diversity.py` | Samples n sequences without replacement and computes S, π, θ_W and Tajima's D. `average_sample_stats` averages them over many populations at chosen generations; `sample_stats_per_trial` keeps each population's values. `tajima_critical_values` gives the limits of Tajima's test, and `control_limits` the limits from simulated steady populations. `sample_stats_and_sfs` also averages the site frequency spectrum, and `sfs_ratio` compares its shape with a steady population's. |
| `recovery.py` | Compares event populations with one steady control and finds the recovery time: the first generation after which they stay within 4 standard errors of each other. The control can be a different size from the starting population (`control_size`), which `growth_recovery_times` uses to compare grown populations with a control at the new size. `run_in_parallel` runs independent seeds on separate CPU cores; each seed sets its own random numbers, so the results are the same as running them one after another. |
| `inference.py` | Works backwards from one sample: builds the reference table (`build_reference_table`, saved in `inference_cache/`), keeps the closest simulated samples (`infer`), summarizes them (`summarize`) and tests the method on samples with known histories (`validate`). |
| `plots.py` | Draws the figures above. |
| `app.py` | The interactive Streamlit app. |
| `animation.py` | Builds the app's animated Plotly charts (the site frequency spectrum and the spread of D over time), with play and pause buttons, a slider and a time marker. |

content.content:
"""
Works backwards: from one sample of DNA sequences, infers what happened to the
population it came from (steady, a crash or growth), how severe the event was and
how long ago it began.

There is no formula for the chance of a sample's statistics after a crash, but the
simulation can produce examples. So we use Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC)
by rejection:
1. Build a reference table: simulate many populations under a grid of possible
   histories, and record the statistics of one sample from each population every
   few generations, next to the history and time that produced them.
2. Put the observed statistics and every row of the table on a common scale and
   measure how far apart they are.
3. Keep the rows closest to the observation. The histories in those rows show
   which histories could have produced the sample, and how likely each is.

We compare three statistics of a sample: pi (driven by variants at middle
frequencies), S (all variable sites) and the number of singletons (sites carried
by one sampled sequence, the rarest variants). Together they summarize the shape
of the site frequency spectrum, which is where crashes and growth leave their mark.
Tajima's D is a function of pi and S, so it adds nothing new.

Steady, crash and growth start with equal prior odds (1/3 each). Within crashes
and growth, every grid point and every recorded time is equally likely.

Pseudocode

BuildReferenceTable(normalSize, mu, n, crashSizes, crashLengths, growthSizes,
                    growthLength, maxTime, recordEvery, numTrials, seed)
    histories ← steady, every crash (size, length), every growth (end size)
    for every history h (all at once, on different CPU cores)
        SetSeed(seed + h)
        stats ← SampleStatsPerTrial(burnIn + history h, ..., at times 0, recordEvery, ... maxTime)
        for every population and every time
            add a row: kind, crash size, length, end size, time, pi, S, singletons,
                       and which population it came from
    return the rows

Infer(observed, table, numKeep)
    scale ← the standard deviation of each statistic among steady rows
    for every row r
        distance[r] ← sqrt of the sum over statistics of ((r - observed) / scale)^2
    keep the numKeep rows with the smallest distance
    weight each kept row by its kind's prior weight (1/3 split over that kind's rows)
    return the kept rows and their weights

Summarize(kept, weights)
    P(kind) ← the share of weight on each kind
    for crashes: the weighted median and 90% range of strength = length / (2 * size)
                 and of the time since the crash began
    for growth: the same for the size after growth and the time since growth began

Validate(table, numTests)
    for numTests random rows
        remove every row from the same simulated population (so no near-copy remains)
        Infer from the rest, and compare the answer with the row's true history
    report how often the kind is right and how close strength and time are
"""

import inspect
import os
import sys

import numpy as np

import wright_fisher
from diversity import sample_stats_per_trial
from recovery import run_in_parallel

STATS = ["pi", "S", "singletons"]
KINDS = ["steady", "crash", "growth"]
CACHE_DIR = "inference_cache"
# Crash strength classes for reporting: (lowest, highest, name).
STRENGTH_CLASSES = [(0, 0.1, "weak (strength < 0.1)"), (0.1, 0.4, "moderate (0.1-0.4)"),
                    (0.4, 1.01, "strong (0.4-1)"), (1.01, np.inf, "severe (> 1)")]


def make_histories(normal_size: int, crash_sizes: list[int], crash_lengths: list[int],
                   growth_sizes: list[int], growth_length: int, max_time: int) -> list[dict]:
    """
    Lists the possible histories of the reference table.
    Parameters:
    - normal_size (int): The population size before any event.
    - crash_sizes (list[int]): The population sizes a crash can drop to.
    - crash_lengths (list[int]): How many generations a crash can last.
    - growth_sizes (list[int]): The population sizes growth can end at.
    - growth_length (int): How many generations growth takes.
    - max_time (int): How many generations to follow after each event begins.
    Returns:
    - list[dict]: One dict per history with "kind", "crash_size", "crash_length",
      "end_size" (0 where they do not apply) and "sizes" (the population size in
      each generation after the burn-in).
    """
    histories = [{"kind": "steady", "crash_size": 0, "crash_length": 0, "end_size": 0,
                  "sizes": [normal_size] * max_time}]
    for size in crash_sizes:
        for length in crash_lengths:
            histories.append({
                "kind": "crash", "crash_size": size, "crash_length": length, "end_size": 0,
                "sizes": wright_fisher.make_crash_history(normal_size, size, 0, length,
                                                          max_time - length)})
    for end_size in growth_sizes:
        histories.append({
            "kind": "growth", "crash_size": 0, "crash_length": 0, "end_size": end_size,
            "sizes": wright_fisher.make_growth_history(normal_size, end_size, 0, growth_length,
                                                       max_time - growth_length)})
    return histories


def _simulate_history(task: tuple) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """
    Simulates one history of the reference table (run by run_in_parallel).
    Parameters:
    - task (tuple): seed, normal_size, sizes, mu, sample_size, num_trials, times.
    Returns:
    - dict[str, np.ndarray]: For each statistic in STATS, one row per population
      and one column per time.
    """
    seed, normal_size, sizes, mu, sample_size, num_trials, times = task
    wright_fisher.set_seed(seed)
    burn_in = [normal_size] * (10 * normal_size)
    stats = sample_stats_per_trial(burn_in + sizes, mu, sample_size, num_trials,
                                   [len(burn_in) + t for t in times])
    return {name: stats[name] for name in STATS}


def build_reference_table(normal_size: int = 200, mu: float = 0.0125, sample_size: int = 20,
                          crash_sizes: tuple = (10, 20, 40, 100),
                          crash_lengths: tuple = (5, 10, 20, 40),
                          growth_sizes: tuple = (400, 1000, 2000, 4000),
                          growth_length: int = 20, max_time: int = 1000,
                          record_every: int = 10, num_trials: int = 200, seed: int = 1,
                          workers: int | None = None) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """
    Simulates every history in the grid and records one sample per population at
    every recorded time.
    Parameters:
    - normal_size (int): The population size before any event (and of steady rows).
    - mu (float): The mutation rate per gene copy per generation.
    - sample_size (int): The number of sampled sequences n.
    - crash_sizes, crash_lengths, growth_sizes, growth_length: The grid of histories
      (see make_histories). Crash sizes must be at least n / 2, so that a sample of
      n sequences can be taken during the crash.
    - max_time (int): How many generations after the event began to follow.
    - record_every (int): How many generations apart to sample.
    - num_trials (int): Populations simulated per history.
    - seed (int): History h uses seed + h, so the table is reproducible.
    - workers (int | None): As in run_in_parallel.
    Returns:
    - dict[str, np.ndarray]: One entry per row for "kind" (index into KINDS),
      "crash_size", "crash_length", "end_size", "time" (generations since the event
      began; nan for steady rows), "population" (which simulated population the row
      came from) and every statistic in STATS. "settings" holds the arguments.
    """
    if any(2 * size < sample_size for size in crash_sizes):
        raise ValueError("Every crash size must be at least sample_size / 2.")
    if any(length >= max_time for length in crash_lengths) or growth_length >= max_time:
        raise ValueError("Events must be shorter than max_time.")

    histories = make_histories(normal_size, list(crash_sizes), list(crash_lengths),
                               list(growth_sizes), growth_length, max_time)
    times = list(range(0, max_time + 1, record_every))
    tasks = [(seed + h, normal_size, history["sizes"], mu, sample_size, num_trials, times)
             for h, history in enumerate(histories)]
    results = run_in_parallel(_simulate_history, tasks, workers)

    rows_per_history = num_trials * len(times)
    table = {}
    for name in ["kind", "crash_size", "crash_length", "end_size"]:
        values = [KINDS.index(h["kind"]) if name == "kind" else h[name] for h in histories]
        table[name] = np.repeat(values, rows_per_history)
    time = np.tile(np.array(times, dtype=float), num_trials * len(histories))
    table["time"] = np.where(table["kind"] == KINDS.index("steady"), np.nan, time)
    table["population"] = np.repeat(np.arange(num_trials * len(histories)), len(times))
    for name in STATS:
        # Each result has one row per population; ravel keeps a population's times together.
        table[name] = np.concatenate([result[name].ravel() for result in results])
    table["settings"] = np.array([normal_size, mu, sample_size, max_time, record_every,
                                  num_trials, seed], dtype=float)
    return table


def cached_reference_table(**kwargs) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """
    Loads a reference table from inference_cache/ if one was built with the same
    arguments, and otherwise builds it and saves it there.
    Parameters:
    - kwargs: As in build_reference_table (except workers, which does not change it).
    Returns:
    - dict[str, np.ndarray]: The table.
    """
    workers = kwargs.pop("workers", None)
    # Include the defaults too, so changing a default never loads a stale table.
    settings = inspect.signature(build_reference_table).bind(**kwargs)
    settings.apply_defaults()
    settings = {name: value for name, value in settings.arguments.items() if name != "workers"}
    key = "_".join(f"{name}-{settings[name]}" for name in sorted(settings))
    key = key.replace(" ", "").replace("(", "").replace(")", "").replace(",", "-")
    path = os.path.join(CACHE_DIR, f"table_{key}.npz")
    if os.path.exists(path):
        with np.load(path) as saved:
            return dict(saved)
    table = build_reference_table(**settings, workers=workers)
    os.makedirs(CACHE_DIR, exist_ok=True)
    np.savez_compressed(path, **table)
    return table


def steady_scale(table: dict[str, np.ndarray]) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Finds how much each statistic varies among steady populations, used to put
    the statistics on a common scale.
    Parameters:
    - table (dict): A reference table.
    Returns:
    - np.ndarray: The standard deviation of each statistic in STATS among steady rows.
    """
    steady = table["kind"] == KINDS.index("steady")
    return np.array([np.std(table[name][steady]) for name in STATS])


def infer(observed: dict[str, float], table: dict[str, np.ndarray], num_keep: int = 500,
          exclude: np.ndarray | None = None) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """
    Keeps the reference rows whose statistics are closest to the observed sample.
    Parameters:
    - observed (dict[str, float]): The observed value of every statistic in STATS.
    - table (dict): A reference table.
    - num_keep (int): How many of the closest rows to keep.
    - exclude (np.ndarray | None): True for rows that may not be kept (used in
      validation to remove the tested population).
    Returns:
    - dict[str, np.ndarray]: The kept rows (every column of the table except
      "settings"), their "distance" and "weight": the prior weight of the row's kind,
      normalized so the weights add up to 1.
    """
    scale = steady_scale(table)
    distance = np.sqrt(sum(((table[name] - observed[name]) / s) ** 2
                           for name, s in zip(STATS, scale)))
    if exclude is not None:
        distance = np.where(exclude, np.inf, distance)
    keep = np.argpartition(distance, num_keep)[:num_keep]
    kept = {name: values[keep] for name, values in table.items() if name != "settings"}
    kept["distance"] = distance[keep]

    # Equal prior odds for each kind: each kind's prior is spread over its rows.
    rows_of_kind = np.bincount(table["kind"], minlength=len(KINDS))
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore"):
        prior = np.where(rows_of_kind > 0, 1 / rows_of_kind, 0)
    weight = prior[kept["kind"]]
    kept["weight"] = weight / weight.sum()
    return kept


def weighted_quantiles(values: np.ndarray, weights: np.ndarray,
                       quantiles: list[float]) -> list[float]:
    """
    Finds quantiles of values in which each value counts with its weight.
    Parameters:
    - values (np.ndarray): The values.
    - weights (np.ndarray): A non-negative weight for each value.
    - quantiles (list[float]): The quantiles wanted, each between 0 and 1.
    Returns:
    - list[float]: One value per quantile, or nan for each if the weights add to 0.
    """
    if len(values) == 0 or weights.sum() <= 0:
        return [np.nan] * len(quantiles)
    order = np.argsort(values)
    cumulative = np.cumsum(weights[order]) / weights.sum()
    return [float(values[order][min(np.searchsorted(cumulative, q), len(values) - 1)])
            for q in quantiles]


def summarize(kept: dict[str, np.ndarray]) -> dict:
    """
    Summarizes the kept rows into probabilities and estimates.
    Parameters:
    - kept (dict): The output of infer.
    Returns:
    - dict: "probability" (of each kind), and for "crash" and "growth" (if they
      have any weight) the median and 90% range of the estimates: for a crash,
      "strength" (length / (2 * size)), "crash_size", "crash_length" and "time";
      for growth, "end_size" and "time". Each estimate is (low, median, high).
    """
    weight = kept["weight"]
    summary = {"probability": {kind: float(weight[kept["kind"] == k].sum())
                               for k, kind in enumerate(KINDS)}}
    for kind, names in [("crash", ["strength", "crash_size", "crash_length", "time"]),
                        ("growth", ["end_size", "time"])]:
        rows = kept["kind"] == KINDS.index(kind)
        if weight[rows].sum() <= 0:
            continue
        estimates = {}
        for name in names:
            if name == "strength":
                values = kept["crash_length"][rows] / (2 * kept["crash_size"][rows])
            else:
                values = kept[name][rows]
            estimates[name] = tuple(weighted_quantiles(values.astype(float), weight[rows],
                                                       [0.05, 0.5, 0.95]))
        summary[kind] = estimates
    return summary


def describe(summary: dict) -> str:
    """
    Writes a summary in words.
    Parameters:
    - summary (dict): The output of summarize.
    Returns:
    - str: A few lines of text.
    """
    p = summary["probability"]
    lines = [f"P(steady) = {p['steady']:.2f}, P(crash) = {p['crash']:.2f}, "
             f"P(growth) = {p['growth']:.2f}"]
    if "crash" in summary and p["crash"] > 0.05:
        c = summary["crash"]
        lines.append(f"  If a crash: strength {c['strength'][1]:.2f} "
                     f"(90%: {c['strength'][0]:.2f} to {c['strength'][2]:.2f}), "
                     f"began {c['time'][1]:.0f} generations ago "
                     f"(90%: {c['time'][0]:.0f} to {c['time'][2]:.0f})")
    if "growth" in summary and p["growth"] > 0.05:
        g = summary["growth"]
        lines.append(f"  If growth: to N = {g['end_size'][1]:.0f} "
                     f"(90%: {g['end_size'][0]:.0f} to {g['end_size'][2]:.0f}), "
                     f"began {g['time'][1]:.0f} generations ago "
                     f"(90%: {g['time'][0]:.0f} to {g['time'][2]:.0f})")
    return "\n".join(lines)


def observe(sizes: list[int], normal_size: int, mu: float, sample_size: int,
            seed: int) -> dict[str, float]:
    """
    Simulates one population with a known history and takes one sample at the end,
    as a test observation.
    Parameters:
    - sizes (list[int]): The population size in each generation after the burn-in.
    - normal_size (int): The burn-in population size.
    - mu (float): The mutation rate per gene copy per generation.
    - sample_size (int): The number of sampled sequences n.
    - seed (int): The random seed.
    Returns:
    - dict[str, float]: The sample's value of every statistic in STATS.
    """
    wright_fisher.set_seed(seed)
    burn_in = [normal_size] * (10 * normal_size)
    stats = sample_stats_per_trial(burn_in + sizes, mu, sample_size, 1,
                                   [len(burn_in) + len(sizes)])
    return {name: float(stats[name][0, 0]) for name in STATS}


def validate(table: dict[str, np.ndarray], num_tests: int = 1000, num_keep: int = 500,
             seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """
    Tests the inference on rows of the table whose history is known. Every row from
    the tested population is removed first, so no near-copy of the test is left.
    Parameters:
    - table (dict): A reference table.
    - num_tests (int): How many rows to test.
    - num_keep (int): As in infer.
    - seed (int): Chooses the test rows.
    Returns:
    - dict[str, np.ndarray]: One entry per test: the true "kind", "time", "strength"
      (nan unless a crash) and "end_size" (0 unless growth), the most probable kind
      ("guess"), the probability given to the true kind ("p_true"), and for crashes
      and growth the median estimates "strength_estimate", "time_estimate" and
      "end_size_estimate" and whether the truth was in the 90% range
      ("strength_covered", "time_covered").
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    # Equal numbers of steady, crash and growth tests.
    tests = np.concatenate([rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(table["kind"] == k),
                                       num_tests // len(KINDS), replace=False)
                            for k in range(len(KINDS))])
    names = ["kind", "guess", "p_true", "time", "strength", "end_size", "strength_estimate",
             "time_estimate", "end_size_estimate", "strength_covered", "time_covered"]
    results = {name: np.full(len(tests), np.nan) for name in names}
    for i, row in enumerate(tests):
        observed = {name: table[name][row] for name in STATS}
        summary = summarize(infer(observed, table, num_keep,
                                  exclude=table["population"] == table["population"][row]))
        kind = KINDS[table["kind"][row]]
        probabilities = summary["probability"]
        results["kind"][i] = table["kind"][row]
        results["guess"][i] = KINDS.index(max(probabilities, key=probabilities.get))
        results["p_true"][i] = probabilities[kind]
        results["time"][i] = table["time"][row]
        results["end_size"][i] = table["end_size"][row]
        if kind == "crash":
            strength = table["crash_length"][row] / (2 * table["crash_size"][row])
            results["strength"][i] = strength
            if "crash" in summary:
                low, median, high = summary["crash"]["strength"]
                results["strength_estimate"][i] = median
                results["strength_covered"][i] = low <= strength <= high
        if kind in ("crash", "growth") and kind in summary:
            low, median, high = summary[kind]["time"]
            results["time_estimate"][i] = median
            results["time_covered"][i] = low <= table["time"][row] <= high
            if kind == "growth":
                results["end_size_estimate"][i] = summary["growth"]["end_size"][1]
    return results


def describe_validation(results: dict[str, np.ndarray]) -> str:
    """
    Summarizes validate's results in words.
    Parameters:
    - results (dict): The output of validate.
    Returns:
    - str: A few lines of text.
    """
    lines = []
    for k, kind in enumerate(KINDS):
        rows = results["kind"] == k
        lines.append(f"{kind:>7}: right kind {np.mean(results['guess'][rows] == k):.0%} of the "
                     f"time (average probability on the truth {np.mean(results['p_true'][rows]):.2f})")
    # Mild crashes look almost exactly like steady populations, so crash detection
    # is shown separately for each strength, early and late.
    crash_rows = results["kind"] == 1
    for low, high, name in STRENGTH_CLASSES:
        cells = []
        for start, end in [(0, 300), (300, 600), (600, 1001)]:
            window = (crash_rows & (results["strength"] >= low) & (results["strength"] < high)
                      & (results["time"] >= start) & (results["time"] < end))
            right = f"{np.mean(results['guess'][window] == 1):.0%}" if window.any() else "-"
            cells.append(f"{start}-{min(end, 1000)}: {right:>4}")
        lines.append(f"  {name:>27} crash, right kind by generations ago: " + ", ".join(cells))
    growth_rows = results["kind"] == 2
    cells = []
    for start, end in [(0, 300), (300, 600), (600, 1001)]:
        window = growth_rows & (results["time"] >= start) & (results["time"] < end)
        cells.append(f"{start}-{min(end, 1000)}: {np.mean(results['guess'][window] == 2):.0%}")
    lines.append(f"  {'growth':>27}, right kind by generations ago: " + ", ".join(cells))
    crash = (results["kind"] == 1) & ~np.isnan(results["strength_estimate"])
    log_error = np.abs(np.log2(results["strength_estimate"][crash] / results["strength"][crash]))
    lines.append(f"Crash strength: median estimate within a factor of "
                 f"{2 ** np.median(log_error):.2f} of the truth; truth inside the 90% range "
                 f"{np.nanmean(results['strength_covered'][crash]):.0%} of the time")
    for kind, k in [("crash", 1), ("growth", 2)]:
        rows = (results["kind"] == k) & ~np.isnan(results["time_estimate"])
        error = np.abs(results["time_estimate"][rows] - results["time"][rows])
        lines.append(f"{kind.capitalize()} time: median error {np.median(error):.0f} generations; "
                     f"truth inside the 90% range {np.nanmean(results['time_covered'][rows]):.0%} "
                     "of the time")
    return "\n".join(lines)


def main():
    normal_size, mu, sample_size = 200, 0.0125, 20
    print("Building the reference table (cached in inference_cache/ after the first run)...")
    table = cached_reference_table(normal_size=normal_size, mu=mu, sample_size=sample_size)
    print(f"  {len(table['kind'])} reference samples")

    mysteries = {
        "steady": [normal_size] * 300,
        "crash to N = 20 for 20 generations, 200 generations ago":
            wright_fisher.make_crash_history(normal_size, 20, 0, 20, 180),
        "crash to N = 10 for 10 generations, 50 generations ago":
            wright_fisher.make_crash_history(normal_size, 10, 0, 10, 40),
        "growth to N = 2000 over 20 generations, 300 generations ago":
            wright_fisher.make_growth_history(normal_size, 2000, 0, 20, 280),
    }
    print("\nOne sample from each mystery population (seeds not used in the table):")
    for i, (label, sizes) in enumerate(mysteries.items()):
        observed = observe(sizes, normal_size, mu, sample_size, seed=10_000 + i)
        print(f"\nTruth: {label}")
        print(f"  observed pi = {observed['pi']:.2f}, S = {observed['S']:.0f}, "
              f"singletons = {observed['singletons']:.0f}")
        print("  " + describe(summarize(infer(observed, table))).replace("\n", "\n  "))

    print("\nValidation on 1500 samples with known histories:")
    print(describe_validation(validate(table, num_tests=1500)))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) > 1:
        sys.exit("usage: python3 inference.py")
    main()
